newsitem.title: USA: US workforce changes allow for jobs, low inflation.
newsitem.headline: US workforce changes allow for jobs, low inflation.

text.p: A series of small changes in the U.S. workforce rather than a single structural shift best explain the current American economic dream of full employment and low inflation, experts said.

The most striking change is the aging of America and the return to the labor force of older workers -- mainly women with grown-up children -- that provides companies with a large pool of skilled workers at competitive wages, they added.
"I'm skeptical that there are fundamental changes," said Alan Blinder, Professor of Economics at Princeton University.

"It's a lot of incremental changes working in the same direction rather than structural changes, much more a series of evolutions rather than a revolution," added Blinder, a former vice chairman of the Federal Reserve.

"It's largely a story of women, as part of the gradually aging population, the female part of which is more experienced than it was 20 years ago," said Blinder, who added that older workers are traditionally more attached to their jobs.
The jobs data released on Friday supported the notion that America can live with full employment and low inflation as U.S. payroll jobs rose by a whopping 316,000 in July.
With about 14 million U.S. jobs created in the recovery since 1991, wage inflation is mostly absent with average hourly earnings just 3.5 percent above their year-ago levels.

The stunning job creation is luring Americans back to work, boosting the participation rate -- or percentage of adults employed or seeking a job -- to a record 67.1-percent average in the past three months. Data show two-thirds of the recent labor force gains came from the 50-to-59-year-olds.
"It's not that the whole population suddenly aged. It's a spread-out process," stressed Blinder who added the demographic shift is tempering wage inflation.
